records.toxicity_detail: NC State (dedicated Daphne odora profile) rates this species "high" poison severity, with poison symptoms "Unknown, but possibly as in D. mezereum," a suspected toxic principle of "a diterpenoid (mezerein)," and confirms it "Causes Contact Dermatitis." Toxic parts listed are bark, flowers, fruits, leaves, roots, seeds, and stems — this documented toxicity is scoped to humans (page problem tag "Poisonous to Humans"), not to cats or dogs. RHS separately warns the plant is "TOXIC if eaten; skin irritant," advising gloves and protective equipment when handling, and adds a "TOXIC to pets" notice, but that notice names no specific animal (it points readers to a third-party HTA guide rather than stating which pets), so it does not meet this catalog's cat/dog-scoped bar for toxic_to_pets.
unknowns: No admissible source scopes Daphne odora toxicity to cats and/or dogs specifically: NC State's Poison fields are labeled 'Poisonous to Humans' only, and RHS's 'TOXIC to pets' notice names no animal (it just points to an external HTA guide). Per the catalog's scoping rule this is insufficient, so toxic_to_pets is left null rather than set true.

NC State (species page) says the shrub wants soil 'that can dry out between waterings,' while Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder (also a dedicated Daphne odora page) says 'Do not allow soils to dry out' and stresses drought sensitivity reduces bloom — a direct species-specific conflict, so water_regime and water_dry_down_target are left null rather than picking a side.

NC State's own structured Soil Drainage tags for this species are 'Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry' — this doesn't cleanly satisfy the schema's moisture_retentive rule (which requires moist/occasionally-wet tags WITHOUT an occasionally-dry counterpart) or the moderate rule (which requires both occasionally-dry AND occasionally-wet tags), so soil_drainage is left null as genuinely ambiguous.

No admissible source states Daphne odora is grown as an indoor houseplant; every admissible source treats it as a hardy outdoor/landscape shrub (NC State gives USDA hardiness zones 7a-9b). Because of this, is_houseplant, day/night temperature ranges, humidity targets, light in foot-candles, and fertilizing schedule/strength are all left null — none of the admissible sources address houseplant-style indoor care for this species.

No admissible source gives a numeric soil pH range for this species; RHS and Missouri Botanical Garden mention only qualitative pH ('alkaline or neutral', 'neutral pH'), so soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max are left null.

Missouri Botanical Garden states this shrub is 'only winter hardy to about 10°F' — that is a freeze-survival threshold, not a stated damage-onset temperature, so per the catalog rule against using survival thresholds for chill_damage_f, it was not used and chill_damage_f is left null.

direct_sun_hours_max is left null: NC State's only hour figures ('6 or more hours', '2-6 hours') come from its site-wide light-category legend embedded in the Light tag field, which is explicitly excluded as a source for this field, and no other admissible source gives species-specific sun-hour prose.
No admissible source provided any fertilizing information (interval, active months, or strength) for this species.

outdoor_sun_exposure — FLAGGED on audit (left as-is, needs manual review before landing): The entry in doubt is "full_sun". "part_shade" should stay -- all three sources carry it (NC State tag "Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)", RHS Position "Full sun, Partial shade", MOBOT structured "Sun: Part shade"). "full_sun" is contradicted by the dedicated MOBOT species page in prose the record already had open: Culture reads "Where winter hardy, this shrub is best grown in moist, rich, sandy-humusy, well-drained soils with a neutral pH in part shade. Avoid full sun (leaves will scorch) in hot summer climates." and Problems reads "Daphnes in the St. Louis area often suffer significant winter injury in severe winters, particularly if improperly planted in locations exposed to cold winter winds and full sun." MOBOT's structured Sun field is "Part shade" alone. In fairness both ways: NC State's own prose does say "Daphne should be planted in sun to part shade..." and RHS lists Full sun, so full_sun is not baseless -- but the record asserts it with zero disclosure while disclosing the water conflict drawn from the *same MOBOT paragraph*, which is a selective-disclosure defect on a field that drives care advice (scorch and winter injury). Repair either way: drop "full_sun" leaving ["part_shade"], or keep it and add an unknowns entry disclosing verbatim that MOBOT says "Avoid full sun (leaves will scorch) in hot summer climates" and lists Sun: Part shade.

outdoor_sun_exposure narrowed to part_shade: NC State's Light tags and RHS's Position both list full sun, but MOBOT's dedicated species page says 'Avoid full sun (leaves will scorch) in hot summer climates', notes winter injury on sites exposed to full sun, and its structured Sun field is 'Part shade' alone -- scorch and winter injury are harm-relevant, so the contested value is left out.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: Refuted on the VALUE, not just a citation defect. Two problems. (1) The quotes do not say what the claims say. The first citation's claim asserts NC State "lists Good Drainage and Moist with no occasionally-dry tag" but supplies only the quote "Good Drainage" — which read alone argues the opposite direction. The second citation's claim is "the Moist tag has no accompanying occasionally-dry tag" supported by the quote "Moist"; an absence is not quotable, so the quote cannot establish the claim. The underlying tag reading is at least accurate — the live page's structured field is exactly "Soil Drainage: Good Drainage / Moist" with no Occasionally Dry or Occasionally Wet. (2) The value itself is wrong for this catalog and risky for this species. I checked the catalog's own established convention by scanning app/data/verified/*.json for records whose soil_drainage citation quotes the bare 'Good Drainage + Moist' pair with no Occasionally tag: 27 records map it to "moderate", only 8 to "moisture_retentive", and b14-annual-flowers2.json declines it outright ('NC State tags the soil as both "Good Drainage" and "Moist"... this doesn't map cleanly onto a single fast/moderate/moisture_retentive value without interpretation, so left null'). The dominant convention for this exact tag pair is moderate. More important, all four species-specific sources emphasize drainage, two with explicit harm warnings the record never weighed: RHS's Cultivation reads "Grow in moderately fertile, moist but well drained, acid soil; will not tolerate chalk soils or waterlogging" and its structured Moisture field is "Moist but well–drained"; Clemson HGIC states "Water-logged soils will lead to root rot" and gives Soil as "Well-drained, rich in organic matter"; MBG says "Best grown in organically rich, slightly acidic, medium moisture, well-drained soil" and lists "Dieback (phytophthora)" among its Problems; NC State's own prose says "moist, well-drained." This is the same real-harm pattern this catalog already used to reverse Rose Moss in b41-grasses-and-groundcovers.json and to remove moisture_retentive in b24-trees-and-more.json ('the species is characterized as well-drained (with consistent moisture), not as retaining/poorly-draining soil'). Recommending a moisture-retentive medium for a phytophthora-susceptible Ericaceae shrub is an affirmatively harmful value. Correct value: "moderate" per the catalog's 27-to-8 convention for this tag pair, or null if the tension is judged irreconcilable — not moisture_retentive.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: Refuted on one specific, correctable defect in a safety field: the prose asserts a plant-part scope RHS does not state, and it does so in the direction of broadening a hazard claim. The record says "RHS separately confirms the whole plant is harmful if eaten by pets including dogs and cats." I fetched the RHS page raw; its entire Potentially harmful block reads: "Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. Pets (dogs, cats, rabbits, rodents, tortoises): Harmful if eaten - For further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants". RHS gives NO part scoping at all — "the whole plant" is the record's addition, and it directly conflicts with the only source that does scope parts (NC State: "Poison Part: Flowers / Leaves / Sap/Juice"). Corrected wording for that clause: "RHS separately states the plant is 'Harmful if eaten', without scoping which parts, and lists pets (dogs, cats, rabbits, rodents, tortoises) as harmed if eaten; it also warns to 'Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling.'" Everything else in this field checks out and should be kept. The symptom list is reproduced COMPLETELY and in order against NC State's live Poison Symptoms field, which reads verbatim: "The leaves and nectar are poisonous. Tingling sensation, salivation, nose running, eyes watering, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, abdominal pain, headache, cardiac failure, weakness, and convulsions; may be fatal." — nothing trimmed, and the RHS handling warning is carried. Three further assertions in the field are uncited-but-true and should gain a citation at repair time rather than be dropped; the page's real strings are: "Poison Severity: High", "Poison Toxic Principle: Andromedotoxin, Grayanotoxins", and "Poison Part: Flowers Leaves Sap/Juice" (all on https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/pieris-japonica/common-name/japanese-pieris/, and the fourth animal, children, is real too — "#problem for children" is in that page's Tags row, though note it is NOT in the Problems list, which stops at cats/dogs/horses).

records.name_note: Admissible sources disagree on which genus name is currently accepted. NC State Extension's dedicated page is titled Berberis aquifolium and lists Mahonia aquifolium under a "Previously known as" heading; Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder similarly calls Berberis aquifolium "Synonymous with and formerly called Mahonia aquifolium" -- both treating Berberis aquifolium as current. RHS runs the opposite direction: its Mahonia aquifolium page gives a Name Status of "Correct", while its separate Berberis aquifolium page gives a Name Status of "Synonym" -- treating Mahonia aquifolium as the accepted name. This is a genuinely different species from Japanese Barberry (Berberis thunbergii), already in this catalog.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension rates this a low-severity poison and tags it non-toxic for cats and dogs (and horses) while also tagging it '#poisonous if ingested': ingestion may cause minor illnesses such as vomiting or diarrhea, the toxic principle is berberine (a benzylisoquinoline alkaloid), it does not cause contact dermatitis, and NC State's Edibility field says the berries are 'Not poisonous, but ... contain berberine that can cause stomach upset, especially with children.' Sources disagree on the berries: NC State and Missouri Botanical Garden call the fruit edible (MOBOT: sour fresh, 'excellent jellies'), while RHS says 'Berries are ornamental; not to be eaten' and advises gloves and protective equipment when handling.
unknowns: scientific_name_accepted left null: admissible sources are split on which name is current. NC State Extension and Missouri Botanical Garden both currently accept Berberis aquifolium (Mahonia aquifolium listed as the former/synonym name). RHS accepts Mahonia aquifolium (Name Status: Correct) and lists Berberis aquifolium as a synonym. See name_note.

soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State Extension's structured pH field lists both 'Acid (<6.0)' and 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' categories without a single defined numeric range, and Missouri Botanical Garden only says 'acidic' qualitatively -- no admissible source gives a clean numeric pH range for this species specifically.

water_regime left null: no admissible source gives a species-specific dry-down statement (e.g. keep moist vs. dry between waterings) beyond general moisture/drainage soil descriptions and NC State's #drought-tolerant tag, which conflict enough that picking an enum value would be a guess. Missouri Botanical Garden's 'Water: Medium' tag also does not map cleanly onto the available enum.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: REFUTED — wrong enum token, and the contradiction is undisclosed. The valid tokens are fast | moderate | moisture_retentive (garden-gnome/app/models/models.py:150-153, SoilDrainage), so "moisture_retentive" is well-formed but is the wet end of a three-point scale, and every source that speaks to drainage puts this species in the middle. Live-checked: NC State's dedicated structured field renders "Soil Drainage:" / "Good Drainage" — the single most on-point structured field available, and it appears nowhere in the record, not in the field, not in a citation, not in unknowns. RHS's structured Moisture field reads "Moist but well–drained or Well–drained". RHS Cultivation, verbatim: "Grow in humus-rich moist but well-drained soil, suited to full or partial shade in a sheltered position but tolerant of sun if soil is not too dry." MOBOT Culture, verbatim: "Grow in moist, organically rich, acidic, well-drained soils in part shade to full shade." Both cited quotes are byte-exact, so nothing is fabricated — the defect is in the reading. The RHS citation's claim label converts "moist BUT well-drained" into "i.e. a moisture-retentive soil rather than a sharp-draining one", which drops the hedge and lets the first half of a two-sided formula govern a field the second half is actually about; the MOBOT citation repeats the same move ("reinforcing a moisture-retentive rather than fast-draining regime" — but "well-drained" is not the opposite of fast-draining, it is the midpoint). CORRECT VALUE: "moderate", cited to NC State's "Soil Drainage: Good Drainage" with RHS's "Moist but well–drained or Well–drained" as corroboration. The humus-rich/moisture-holding half of the sources' advice is already carried by soil_base=garden_bed and belongs in prose, not in the drainage enum. If instead the field is nulled, an unknowns entry must be added naming the NC State "Good Drainage" field explicitly.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: REFUTED as an incomplete safety field, on four counts; the facts it does state are all true and verbatim-checkable, so this is a completeness/disclosure defect, not a fabrication. (a) SELECTIVE TAG LIST. The field reproduces three tags from NC State's tag block ("#non-toxic for cats", "#non-toxic for horses", "#non-toxic for dogs" — all three verbatim) but silently drops the co-listed "#poisonous if ingested" tag from that same block, and omits "Poison Severity:" / "Low". Presenting part of a tag list as though it were the list is the exact defect class flagged; the page's own summary line, verbatim, is "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." (b) MISSING THE MOST CONSUMER-RELEVANT SENTENCE. NC State's Edibility field reads, verbatim: "Not poisonous, but berries contain berberine that can cause stomach upset, especially with children." That is the only child-specific warning on any of the three pages and it is absent from the record. (c) UNDISCLOSED SOURCE CONFLICT ON BERRY EDIBILITY. The field carries only RHS's prohibition ("Berries are ornamental; not to be eaten.  Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling" — I confirmed this is byte-exact including the double space, it is in the RHS source HTML under "Potentially harmful"), while both other admissible sources call the fruit edible: NC State's "Fruit Value To Gardener: Edible" plus the Edibility sentence above, and MOBOT's "Fruit: Showy, Edible" plus "Berries are somewhat sour fresh off the plant, but make excellent jellies and are attractive to birds." A safety field that reproduces one source's prohibition without the direct contradiction from the other two is misleading in the direction of false confidence about a source disagreement. (d) CITATION DEFECT ON A LOAD-BEARING SAFETY CLAIM. The citation labeled "NC State Extension states this species does not cause contact dermatitis, and lists poisonous parts as bark, leaves, roots, and sap/juice" is backed by the one-word quote "Bark", which supports neither half of the claim. "Bark" does appear on the page under "Poison Part:", so this is not fabricated, but it is not load-bearing. NC State renders these as label/value pairs on separate elements; substitute two citations quoting "Causes Contact Dermatitis:" → "No" and "Poison Part:" → "Bark / Leaves / Roots / Sap/Juice". Separately, the "#non-toxic for horses" clause in the field prose has no citation at all (only cats and dogs are cited) — uncited-but-true, the tag "#non-toxic for horses" is verbatim on the page; add it or drop the clause. water_regime — removed on audit: REFUTED. Structural check passes (citation 9's label contains "water_regime") and the quote is verbatim, but the quote is about SOIL CHARACTER, not watering cadence -- "moist, organically rich, well-drained soils" describes the medium to plant into, and the enum was read off the adjective "moist". The same MOBOT paragraph, two sentences later, says the opposite of keep_moist: "Established plants have very good drought tolerance." and "Avoid overly moist to wet soils." MOBOT's own structured field reads "Water: Medium", not high. NC State lists Drought under "Resistance To Challenges" and describes moisture as "moist to occasionally dry or wet conditions". RHS Cultivation: "Will grow in almost any soil or situation except soil prone to waterlogging, tolerating full shade, dry soil, pollution and salt wind." A species with a Medium water rating, explicit established drought tolerance, and an explicit warning against overly moist soils is not keep_moist. This is also inconsistent handling of one sentence: the record correctly nulled soil_drainage BECAUSE of "Avoid overly moist to wet soils", then ignored that same clause when setting water_regime from the same sentence's other half. Repair: either set water_regime to the moderate/medium token (MOBOT "Water: Medium"), or null it and disclose the conflict the way soil_drainage's was. If the value is kept, MOBOT's caveats must be disclosed in `unknowns`; right now the hedge is silently dropped. Supporting quote for a moderate reading, verbatim Clemson: "The ideal soil is moist, high in organic matter and well-drained, although it will tolerate almost any soil condition."

outdoor_sun_exposure — FLAGGED on audit (left as-is, needs manual review before landing): REFUTED on one entry only. "part_shade" and "full_shade" should STAY -- they are supported by all four sources independently. "full_sun" should GO. It rests entirely on RHS's structured Position tag, which is a UK-climate generality, and is contradicted by every species-specific statement on the other pages, including a source the record consulted but never cited. NC State's Light tags contain NO full-sun tag at all (only Dappled Sunlight, Deep shade, Partial Shade), and its prose says: "Partial shade to deep shade is the best growing environment. Young leaves exposed to the sun will blacken." MOBOT's structured Sun field reads "Part shade to full shade" -- full sun is absent -- and its Culture says: "Plants in hot summer climates perform best with plenty of shade, particularly from afternoon sun (young leaves are susceptible to burning)." Clemson HGIC is blunter still: "The biggest problem with aucuba is foliage burn when exposed to full sun, and this can be avoided with proper plant placement." and "Aucuba should be planted in partial to full shade (summer and winter), as its leaves will 'burn' in summer and turn sickly green in winter." RHS itself publishes a problem page titled "Aucuba blackening". Three of four sources, including both structured tag sets other than RHS's, exclude full sun; one source's tag cannot outvote them. Flagging the doubt in `unknowns` does not license shipping the value -- the app surfaces the list, not the caveat. Repair: outdoor_sun_exposure = ["part_shade", "full_shade"], drop citation 6 or re-scope its claim to part/full shade only, and add a Clemson citation (https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/aucuba/) carrying the verbatim burn sentence above, since Clemson is currently leaned on in `unknowns` with no citation entry.

records.cool_rest_note: Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder advises watering regularly during the growing season but substantially reducing watering from fall to late winter, consistent with the plant's preference for cool temperatures.
records.name_note: NC State Extension lists several common names in current use for this species -- Big-leaf Paper Plant, Fatsia, Glossy-Leaved Paper Plant, Japanese Aralia, Japanese Fatsia, and Paper Plant -- while RHS's page, whose lead name is Japanese aralia, separately lists castor oil plant, fatsi, fig-leaf palm, and glossy-leaved paper plant under its secondary "Other common names" field, with Aralia japonica and Aralia sieboldii (in two authority spellings) recorded as historical synonyms of the accepted botanical name.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension tags Fatsia japonica as non-toxic for cats, non-toxic for dogs, and non-toxic for horses. Separately, RHS's Potentially harmful section notes: "Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling," and its Pets field states "Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers" -- this RHS caution does not name cats or dogs specifically or describe any symptoms, so it is a general handling/eating caution rather than toxicity evidence, and does not override the NC State non-toxic tags.
unknowns: outdoor_sun_exposure: RHS's structured 'Position' field lists Full sun as a tolerated exposure, but both NC State Extension ('the leaves will brown if it is sited in full sun or with wind exposure') and Clemson HGIC ('Excessive wind exposure or full sun will cause leaf injury') give unconditional species-specific warnings against full sun. full_sun was excluded from outdoor_sun_exposure given these two direct warnings; only full_shade and part_shade are recorded.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max left null: NC State's own pH tags span Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0), AND Neutral (6.0-8.0) -- essentially the entire measurable range -- and RHS's pH field similarly reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral.' Neither source narrows to a bounded numeric range, so no min/max was recorded.

soil_drainage: NC State's own raw tags (Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Wet) would mechanically map to moisture_retentive, but NC State's own qualitative statement ('Too much moisture in the soil can cause root rot') plus Clemson's Phytophthora root rot warning in poorly drained sites, and RHS's 'Moist but well-drained' tag, together weigh toward a well-drained requirement despite moisture tolerance -- so moderate was used instead of moisture_retentive, per the instruction to weigh a same-source disease-risk statement over the mechanical tag mapping.

water_regime: UGA CAES's structured cultural-care table (species-specific row for Fatsia japonica / Japanese Aralia, W=2 'Surface of soil mix should dry before re-watering') was used as the primary, enum-mapping source. This conflicts with Missouri Botanical Garden's culture note to 'Water regularly during the growing season,' which reads closer to keep_moist during active growth (with a separate fall-to-winter reduction). Both are species-specific pages; the UGA structured rating was preferred because it maps cleanly to the required enum.

day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max were derived from UGA CAES's temperature legend codes T=1 (Cool) through T=2 (Average) applied to the Fatsia japonica / Japanese Aralia table row (L=3-4, T=1-2, H=2, W=2, S=2 as read directly from the table). Missouri Botanical Garden separately notes the plant 'Likes cool temperatures (60-70°F)' without splitting day vs. night, which is broadly consistent with but not identical to the UGA-derived range; that MOBOT figure was not used for these numeric fields since it isn't day/night-specific.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's only hour figures ('2-6 hours' for Partial Shade, etc.) come from its generic site-wide light-category legend rather than species-specific prose, so per instructions they were not used.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength left null: NC State says to 'Fertilize regularly except in the winter when it is not growing' and Clemson says to 'Fertilize fatsias lightly in the spring once the last frost is past. Use a slow-release tree and shrub fertilizer, such as a 12-6-6' -- neither gives a literal numeric day interval, explicit calendar months, or a dilution/strength fraction (12-6-6 is an NPK formulation, not a strength fraction), so no admissible-source numeric value could be recorded.

water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis left null: no admissible source gives a literal numeric watering-frequency interval (in days) or a soil check depth for this species.

soil_base was inferred narrowly from Missouri Botanical Garden's houseplant/container culture note ('Easily grown in a humusy potting mix'); outdoor garden-bed soil texture tolerances (clay, loam, sand, chalk) are separately documented across sources but the schema allows only one soil_base value, and the houseplant-context potting mix was chosen as most directly supported and enum-appropriate.

chill_damage_f — removed on audit: The cited number is a survival/regional-growing-limit figure being used as a damage-onset threshold, and Clemson draws no such distinction. The full live sentence is: 'It will grow throughout South Carolina with the exception of areas in the mountains that occasionally drop to below 10 degF' -- that is a statement about where the shrub can be grown at all, i.e. the survival edge, not the temperature at which cold damage begins. Two cross-checks confirm 10 degF is the survival band, not the damage band: NC State's structured 'USDA Plant Hardiness Zone: 7b, 8a, 8b, 9a, 9b, 10a, 10b' (7b = 5-10 degF), and RHS's hardiness rating H5, which its own legend defines as 'hardy in most places throughout the UK even in severe winters (-15 to -10)' degC, i.e. roughly 5-14 degF. Meanwhile both US sources document foliage injury from far milder stress ('the leaves will brown if it is sited in full sun or with wind exposure'; 'Excessive wind exposure or full sun will cause leaf injury'), and no admissible source anywhere states a foliage cold-damage onset temperature for this species. This matters because the record is is_houseplant: true -- a chill_damage_f of 10 tells a user their patio or indoor Fatsia is undamaged down to 10 degF, which the sources do not support. I cannot state a corrected figure, because no admissible source publishes one: the correct repair is to null chill_damage_f and add an unknowns line ('chill_damage_f left null: Clemson's only temperature figure, below 10 degF, is a regional growing-range limit and RHS's H5 rating (-15 to -10 degC) is a survival band; neither states a foliage damage-onset temperature'), or, if the field is retained at 10, to disclose in unknowns that it was derived from a survival/range limit rather than a stated damage threshold. As written, the derivation appears in no unknowns entry at all.

scientific_name_accepted — removed on audit: Structural failure: no citation's claim label contains the string 'scientific_name_accepted'. The closest is 'name_note - historical synonym names for the accepted species', which is labeled for name_note, not for this field. The value itself is correct -- RHS's Botanical Details block for this page carries 'Name Status | Correct' for Fatsia japonica, and NC State's dedicated page lists 'Previously known as: Aralia japonica, Aralia sieboldii' -- so the repair is to add a citation labeled for the field rather than to change the value. Substitutable quote from the live RHS page: 'Name Status Correct' (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/7147/fatsia-japonica-japanese-aralia-castor-oil-plant/details), or NC State's 'Previously known as: Aralia japonica, Aralia sieboldii' (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/fatsia-japonica/).

chill_damage_f left null: Clemson's only temperature figure (below 10 degrees F) is a regional growing-range limit, NC State's zone 7b floor and RHS's H5 rating are survival bands, and no admissible source states a foliage cold-damage onset temperature -- both US sources document leaf injury from sun and wind instead.

records.toxicity_detail: Fruits are poisonous. NC State rates poison severity Medium: causes abortion and cardiac arrest in large amounts, while small amounts can cause nausea; NC State adds that the fruits can cause cardiac arrest if ingested in large quantities. The toxic principle is unknown, the affected plant part is the fruits, and it does not cause contact dermatitis. RHS warns that the fruit are ornamental and not to be eaten, and to wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. No admissible source scopes this to cats or dogs specifically.
unknowns: Sources scope Skimmia japonica's fruit toxicity to humans/children (NC State: 'Poisonous to Humans Problem for Children') and to unscoped 'Pets' (RHS: fruit not to be eaten, see HTA guide) without naming cats or dogs specifically, so toxic_to_pets is left null rather than assumed true.

Skimmia japonica is dioecious (separate male and female plants); NC State and Missouri Botanical Garden both note male plants bear larger, showier flowers while only pollinated female plants produce the red berries, and a roughly 1-male-to-6-female planting ratio is recommended for good fruit set.
No admissible source gives a numeric lower bound for soil pH tolerance (only the upper 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' tag from NC State), so soil_ph_min is left null.
No admissible source gives a fertilizing schedule, strength, or active months for Skimmia japonica, so all fertilize_* fields are left null.
This is an outdoor landscape shrub; no admissible source gives indoor-style day/night temperature ranges, ambient humidity needs, or light footcandle values, so those fields are left null.

NC State's light-category tags (Dappled Sunlight, Deep shade, Partial Shade) support the outdoor_sun_exposure values but their hour ranges are generic site-wide legend text, not species-specific prose, so direct_sun_hours_max is left null per the scoping rule.
No admissible source gives explicit watering-interval day counts (growing or dormant season) or a check depth, so those fields are left null.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: REFUTED — wrong enum token, and the supporting citations are self-contradictory. The enum is only three tokens (garden-gnome/app/models/models.py:150-153: fast / moderate / moisture_retentive), so `moisture_retentive` is the WETTEST bucket. All three cited sources say the opposite. NC State (verified live): 'Plant this shrub in rich, acidic, well-drained soils in part to full shade.' MoBot (verified live): 'Best grown in moist, humusy, organically rich, moderately fertile, well-drained soils...' RHS (verified live): 'Grow in humus-rich, light, rich, moist but well-drained soil...' The RHS citation reads the 'moist' half and silently drops 'but well-drained' — a hedge inversion; 'moist but well-drained' is the textbook definition of the MIDDLE token, not the wet one. Separately, the NC State citation quotes only 'Good Drainage' and labels it soil_drainage, so AS QUOTED that citation argues for the opposite of the value it is filed under, and the conflict is nowhere disclosed in unknowns. (For the record, the page's Soil Drainage field actually carries TWO tags — 'Good Drainage' and 'Moist' — and the record quoted only the half that contradicts its own value.) Corpus precedent confirms the reading: across the 229 verified records that set this field, moisture_retentive is reserved for genuinely wet-loving things (Spinach, Cucumber, Green Beans, Buttercup) while ordinary well-drained woody plants land moderate (American Beech, Eastern Cottonwood, Chinese Fringe Flower). CORRECT VALUE: `moderate`. Repair the NC State citation to quote the full tag pair 'Good Drainage' + 'Moist', or better, quote the prose sentence above.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: REFUTED — safety field is trimmed of a handling warning that one of the record's OWN cited sources carries. The NC State symptom list is reproduced completely and accurately (verified verbatim on the live page: Poison Severity 'Medium'; Poison Symptoms 'Causes abortion, cardiac arrest in large amounts. Small amounts can cause nausea.'; Poison Toxic Principle 'Unknown.'; Causes Contact Dermatitis 'No'; Poison Part 'Fruits'). But RHS's 'Potentially harmful' block reads in full: 'Fruit are ornamental; not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. Pets: Fruit are ornamental; not to be eaten - see the HTA guide...' The record's RHS citation quote begins at 'Pets:', cropping out exactly the PPE instruction, and toxicity_detail carries no handling guidance at all. NC State also supplies two uncited-but-true reinforcements: the Edibility field, 'The fruits are poisonous and can cause cardiac arrest if ingested in large quantities.', and the description sentence, 'The attractive red berries are poisonous and should not be ingested.' CORRECTED WORDING: 'Fruits are poisonous. NC State rates poison severity Medium: causes abortion and cardiac arrest in large amounts, while small amounts can cause nausea; NC State adds that the fruits can cause cardiac arrest if ingested in large quantities. The toxic principle is unknown, the affected plant part is the fruits, and it does not cause contact dermatitis. RHS warns that the fruit are ornamental and not to be eaten, and to wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling.' Also extend the RHS citation quote leftward to start at 'Fruit are ornamental' so the PPE sentence is actually cited.

water_regime — removed on audit: REFUTED on citation integrity and an undisclosed species-specific conflict; the VALUE probably survives repair. (a) The claim label asserts MoBot's notes 'call for consistently moist soil'. The word 'consistently' appears nowhere on the live page, and the quoted sentence is a description of soil COMPOSITION ('moist, humusy, organically rich, moderately fertile, well-drained soils'), not a watering cadence — an inserted intensifier that upgrades a soil adjective into a regime instruction. (b) MoBot's own species-specific structured watering statement is 'Water: Medium' — that is the page's actual watering rating, it is a moderate call, and it is not disclosed anywhere in the record. This is exactly the 'more species-specific source contradicts the chosen value, conflict undisclosed' case. (c) keep_moist remains defensible on the other evidence (NC State's Soil Drainage tag set includes 'Moist'; RHS 'moist but well-drained'), and this is the sole citation for the field, so it cannot lean on a clean sibling. REPAIR: relabel to 'water_regime: Missouri Botanical Garden specifies moist, humusy, organically rich, well-drained soils for Skimmia japonica', add an unknowns line disclosing that MoBot's structured tag rates it 'Water: Medium' while the prose and RHS both say moist, and keep keep_moist only if the project reads 'moist but well-drained' as keep_moist elsewhere.

water_regime keep_moist rests on MOBOT's and RHS's 'moist ... well-drained' soil prescriptions and NC State's Moist tag; MOBOT's structured watering field rates it 'Water: Medium', disclosed here as a moderate counterpoint.

normalizations: 2026-09-02: twenty-ninth batch, the first at the overnight throttle (6 species, research on Sonnet at medium effort, verify on Opus) -- a shade-shrub set: Winter Daphne, Japanese Pieris (checked against Rhododendron for grayanotoxin family-level bleed; none), Oregon Grape (left with scientific_name_accepted null on a genuine split -- NC State and MOBOT now file it as Berberis aquifolium, RHS keeps Mahonia aquifolium as Correct), Japanese Aucuba, Japanese Aralia, and Japanese Skimmia. 1.39M subagent tokens for six species, about 30% less per species than b46. land_check.py, covered.py and verify_quotes.py (81/81 reachable quotes) ran clean before and after repair. Winter Daphne's toxic_to_pets is correctly null despite the plant's reputation: NC State's Poison fields are human-scoped and RHS's 'TOXIC to pets' names no animal -- the scoping rule holds even when it is inconvenient. The audit's dominant finding, on three records (Pieris, Oregon Grape, Skimmia), was 'moist but well-drained' being read as the wet end of the soil_drainage scale rather than the middle; all three corrected to moderate on the sources' own well-drained prescriptions (RHS 'will not tolerate waterlogging' for Pieris; NC State's structured 'Good Drainage' for Oregon Grape; NC State's 'well-drained soils' prose for Skimmia) and this catalog's 27-to-8 precedent for the bare Good Drainage + Moist tag pair. Two safety fields were restored complete after the audit found them trimmed: Oregon Grape's now carries NC State's '#poisonous if ingested' tag, its low-severity line, the berberine/children Edibility sentence, and the disclosed NC State/MOBOT-vs-RHS disagreement on whether the berries are edible; Skimmia's now carries RHS's gloves warning (the record had cropped the quote to start at 'Pets:') and NC State's cardiac-arrest Edibility sentence. Pieris's toxicity_detail was reworded so RHS is no longer credited with a 'whole plant' scope it never states. Three outdoor_sun_exposure lists lost full_sun on species-specific scorch/burn evidence (Winter Daphne via MOBOT, Aucuba via NC State, MOBOT and Clemson; Aralia had already excluded it). Aucuba's water_regime was left null on MOBOT's own 'very good drought tolerance' and 'Avoid overly moist to wet soils' against its 'moist' soil adjective; Aralia's chill_damage_f was left null because Clemson's 10°F is a growing-range limit, not a damage onset, and its scientific_name_accepted was restored with an RHS Name Status citation. toxic_to_pets: Pieris true on explicit NC State Problem for Cats/Dogs tags plus RHS naming both; Oregon Grape and Aralia false on explicit non-toxic tags; Daphne, Aucuba and Skimmia null with no cat/dog-scoped source.
